drafts.title: AI training pay hits $400 an hour for experts, but the work can vanish overnight
drafts.summary: AI firms such as micro1, Mercor and Handshake AI are paying doctors, lawyers and scientists up to $400 an hour, but the work is often patchy and contracts can end with little warning.
drafts.body:
Expert AI training work has moved well beyond quick tagging jobs. New reporting from Bloomberg this month shows AI companies offering doctors, lawyers and scientists hourly rates that rival their day jobs, with some postings reaching $400 an hour. The headline numbers are eye-catching, but the same reporting shows the work can be patchy and can end without much warning.

## What the top rates look like

Bloomberg looked at recruiter postings and spoke to people doing this work. A few figures stood out:

- **micro1** postings included software engineers at up to $120 an hour, condensed matter physics experts at $170 an hour and civil rights attorneys at $400 an hour.
- **Mercor** told Bloomberg its average pay is now $110 an hour, though it said it had no data on what share of tasks pay that much.
- **Handshake AI** has advertised physician roles at up to $200 an hour and lawyer roles at $90 to $110 an hour, according to PYMNTS, which also lists a Mercor legal role at $60 to $150 an hour.

LinkedIn reportedly named data annotators the fourth-fastest-growing job in the US this year.

## Most data work still pays far less

Not everyone is earning expert rates. Bloomberg contrasts a radiologist who earns in an hour roughly what a stay-at-home mum doing general data work earns in a week. Researcher Antonio Casilli told Bloomberg that experts are *"just the cherry on top"*, with most data work still done by low-paid workers.

The research platform Prolific said experts now make up 30% of its participants, but did not say how much of the work they actually get.

## The work can stop suddenly

The pay is only half the story. PYMNTS describes a Princeton PhD who took a $70-an-hour Mercor role in January, worked anywhere from 4 to 20 hours a week, and then had the contract ended in mid-March through a Slack message sent to a group of 810 people.

There are other risks to weigh too:

- Hours vary. Projects open and close quickly, and nobody is guaranteed a set number of hours.
- Mercor reportedly faces at least seven class action lawsuits filed in April after a data breach. The suits allege that interview recordings, facial biometric data and screenshots were exposed. Mercor has called the claims speculative and says only a limited group of experts had sensitive data leaked.
- Funding is still flowing. Bloomberg reports Mercor has discussed new funding at a $20 billion valuation and that micro1 is valued at $4 billion, so demand looks set to continue for now.

## What it means for you

If you have a professional qualification, this is a good time to put it to work, as long as you go in with your eyes open:

1. **Lead with your specialism.** The highest rates go to people with deep expertise in law, medicine, science or engineering. Make it the first thing on your profile.
2. **Treat it as extra income, not a salary.** Contracts can end overnight, so keep your main income steady and spread your work across two or three platforms.
3. **Check what you're sharing.** Some platforms record interviews or screens. Read the privacy terms and only share what you need to.
4. **Judge a role by its hourly rate and its hours.** A high rate means little if a project only lasts a fortnight. Ask how long it is expected to run.
5. **Stay alert to fakes.** High advertised rates attract scammers. Real platforms never ask you to pay to join or to buy equipment from them, so apply through the official site.

You can search current expert and generalist AI training roles, filtered by pay, on GigrAI.

sources.title: Bloomberg Law: Doctors and Lawyers Are Joining AI's $400-an-Hour Gig Economy
PYMNTS: AI Labs Pay Lawyers $400 an Hour to Train Models

drafts.title: AI now appears in a record share of job adverts, but pay is lagging prices
drafts.summary: Indeed says 7.3% of US job adverts now mention AI skills, a record high, while advertised pay trails inflation. Here is what that means for AI trainers and remote workers.
drafts.body:
More job adverts than ever now mention artificial intelligence, even as the wider hiring picture stays lukewarm. That's the headline from Indeed Hiring Lab's latest US labour market snapshot, published on 22 October. If you train AI models for a living, or you're hoping to, the numbers say a lot about where demand for AI-literate people is heading.

## AI mentions hit a new high

According to Indeed, AI-related postings now make up **7.3% of all job adverts** on its US site. The previous peak was 3.3%, back in 2022, so the share has more than doubled.

Indeed counts a posting as AI-related when it uses terms such as "machine learning", "data science", "generative AI", "large language models" or "ChatGPT". So this isn't only about AI engineers: plenty of ordinary roles now ask for people who can work with these tools.

## The wider market: steady, not strong

Away from AI, the picture is mixed:

- Overall US postings are almost 4% above their February 2020 level and 2.8% higher than a year ago (a year earlier they were down 8.1%).
- 68% of job sectors now have more openings than a year ago, up from 49% at the start of September.
- Even so, Indeed is cautious. In its words, "it would be premature to say the labor market is strengthening."

Pay is the sore point. Advertised wages rose 2.4% year on year in September, while inflation ran at 3.7%. In other words, posted pay isn't keeping up with prices for most people.

## Winners and losers

Engineering is the stand-out. Mechanical, civil and electrical engineering are among the five strongest sectors, and electrical engineering pay in job adverts is up 5.6% on last year. Postings linked to data centres, the huge buildings that run AI models, have grown another 20% in three months and are now 147% above their June 2024 level.

Software development, by contrast, is the weakest sector Indeed tracks. Tech-heavy cities feel it most, with Seattle and San Francisco among the softest job markets in the country. So "AI is booming" and "tech hiring is weak" are both true at once: companies want AI skills spread across many roles, not simply more developers.

## What it means for you

Indeed's data covers the US, but the trend is a useful signal for remote workers anywhere.

1. **AI skills are becoming a general requirement.** If you already do AI training work, such as rating chatbot answers, writing prompts or checking model reasoning, that's real, relevant experience. Put it on your CV in plain terms: which kinds of tasks, which domains, and roughly how many hours.
2. **Your specialism is your edge.** With engineering and healthcare roles in demand, people with expertise in those fields are well placed for higher-paid expert AI training projects, not just general tasks.
3. **Don't rely on one income stream.** With pay lagging inflation, many people are topping up their earnings. AI training work can fill that gap, but projects come and go, so spread yourself across more than one reputable platform.
4. **Watch out for fake "AI jobs".** When a buzzword is hot, scammers copy it. A genuine platform will never ask you to pay to join, buy a "starter kit" or deposit money to unlock tasks.

You can browse current remote AI training roles from established platforms on [GigrAI](https://remotegigrai.com), all free to search.

drafts.title: Holiday job scams are back: fake mystery shopper offers and recruiters you never contacted
drafts.summary: The BBB warns fake mystery shopper offers are spreading ahead of the holidays, and mass job applications make fake recruiters harder to spot. Here is how to protect yourself.
drafts.body:
It's that time of year again. As people look for extra income before the holidays, fake job offers come back with them. This week the Better Business Bureau (BBB) in the US warned that fake mystery shopper offers are spreading, and a recent Malwarebytes article explains why it's getting harder to tell a real recruiter from a scammer when you've applied to dozens of roles.

If you look for remote or flexible work online, including AI training work, both stories are worth a few minutes of your time.

## The mystery shopper trick

According to the BBB, fake mystery shopper offers turn up every autumn, and the seasonal rise seems to start a little earlier each year. Daniel Irwin of BBB Mid-South told local broadcaster WBBJ that people are being "inundated with these fake offers".

The scam usually works like this:

1. You're offered a mystery shopping "assignment" and sent a cheque, sometimes worth several thousand dollars.
2. You're told to pay it in, keep a slice as your wages, and spend the rest on gift cards for the "employer".
3. Days later the bank finds the cheque is fake. By then the gift card codes have gone to the scammers, and you owe the bank the full amount.

The BBB's advice is simple: never pay in a cheque from a stranger and then send part of the money on, never pay an employer with gift cards, and be very wary of unsolicited offers promising easy money for flexible hours.

## Why mass applying makes scams harder to spot

Malwarebytes raises a less obvious problem. Many job seekers now send out large numbers of applications, often with AI tools, and don't keep track of them. When you're expecting replies from all over the place, a message from a "recruiter" you've never contacted can easily look like a normal reply.

The article points out that this doesn't prove mass applying causes people to fall for scams, but it does make the fakes harder to notice. It cites research commissioned by Virgin Media O2 in which almost half of UK 18 to 24-year-olds surveyed said they'd been offered jobs they never applied for.

Among the tricks it lists:

- **Task scams** that promise big daily earnings for an hour or so of "work", then ask you to deposit money to unlock your pay
- **Fake interview apps** that are really spyware
- **Booking links and sign-in pages** built to steal your social media or Google logins
- **Parcel jobs** that turn you into a money or goods mule

## What it means for you

Real AI training platforms do contact people and do pay for flexible remote work, which is exactly why scammers copy them. A few habits will protect you:

- **Keep a simple log** of every role you apply for: platform, role, date and the original listing. If a message doesn't match anything in it, treat it with suspicion.
- **Check independently.** Go to the company's own website rather than clicking a link in a text, WhatsApp or email. Seeing a logo you recognise is no guarantee.
- **Never pay to get paid.** No genuine platform asks you to deposit money, buy gift cards or pay a "fee" before you can withdraw earnings.
- **Be careful with software and logins.** Don't install apps or sign in through a link a recruiter sends you until you've confirmed they're real.
- **Turn on two-factor authentication** for your email and payment accounts.
- **Report it.** In the US, the BBB Scam Tracker collects reports. Elsewhere, use your national fraud reporting service.

If an offer comes to you out of the blue and the pay sounds too good for the effort, slow down. A real opportunity will still be there after you've checked.

sources.title: WBBJ: BBB warns of mystery shopper scam targeting holiday job seekers
Malwarebytes: "Spray and pray" job applications could make it harder for you to spot a scam

drafts.title: Back in the office, still on Zoom: New York Fed finds many office days are remote in all but name
drafts.summary: A New York Fed study finds roughly half of in-office days are spent entirely on video calls or solo work, and official figures may miss most remote work.
drafts.body:
Plenty of employers have spent the last few years calling staff back to their desks. A new paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York suggests that, for many of those workers, the office day looks a lot like a day at home, just with a commute bolted on.

The study, titled *Remote Work from the Office* and written by economists Natalia Emanuel and Emma Harrington, was published as a New York Fed staff report this month. It is based on a survey of college-educated Americans, plus other data on how teams are spread out.

## What the research found

The headline finding is striking: roughly half of in-office days are spent entirely on video calls or doing solo work. In the authors' words, these workers "commute in just to work remotely from the office".

A few other points stand out:

- **Official figures undercount remote work.** The authors argue that measures which only count working from home miss up to three quarters of how much remote work really happens.
- **Distance is the biggest driver.** Teammates are often based in different offices or work fully remotely, so even people who go in end up on calls.
- **Coordination is patchy.** People don't always follow in-office rules, and teams often fail to line up the same days.
- **Habits stick.** Many people take calls from their desks rather than booking a meeting room, even when everyone is in the same building.

## Why it matters for the return-to-office debate

Return-to-office mandates are usually justified by collaboration: the idea that being together sparks better teamwork. This research doesn't say offices are pointless, but it does suggest that simply requiring attendance doesn't guarantee much face-to-face work.

Forbes, covering the paper, framed it as evidence that office mandates often fall short of their goals, and that how in-office days are planned may matter more than how many there are.

For remote workers, it is also a useful reminder of something many already know: modern work is distributed by default. A team spread across cities, countries and time zones runs on video calls, chat and shared documents, wherever its members happen to be sitting.

## What it means for you

If you work remotely, or want to, including in AI training and other online contract work, here is how to use this:

1. **Treat remote skills as core skills.** Clear written updates, good video-call habits and working across time zones are what distributed teams rely on. Mention them on your profile and in applications.
2. **Don't assume a hybrid job means real teamwork.** If you are weighing an office-based role against remote contract work, ask who your teammates are and where they sit. You may be on calls all day anyway.
3. **Use the research when negotiating.** If an employer is pushing you back in, it is fair to ask what the office days are actually for and how they will be coordinated.
4. **Keep your setup professional.** Since so much work happens over video either way, a reliable connection, a decent headset and a quiet space matter wherever you work.
5. **Stay flexible.** Remote and contract work, including AI training projects, can be stop-start. Building skills that transfer across platforms and teams keeps your options open.

The office isn't going away, but this study is a good sign that the line between "remote" and "in-office" work is much blurrier than the debate suggests.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Bank of New York (Fed in Print): Remote Work from the Office
Federal Reserve Bank of New York: Staff Report 1211, Remote Work from the Office
Forbes: Why Return-To-Office Mandates Fall Short, According To New Research
